We propose Socratic-Geo, a fully autonomous framework                      Figure 1. Inspired by Socratic methodology, our Socratic-Geo
that dynamically couples data synthesis with model learn-                  Framework employs a Teacher (powerful LLM) to guide two
ing through multi-agent interaction. The Teacher agent                     agents from an initial geo-image dataset. The Teacher uses Reflect
generates parameterized Python scripts with reflective feed-               for question quality control and Python tools (RePI) for geometric
back (Reflect for solvability, RePI for visual validity), ensur-           drawing and verification, ensuring accurate image-text alignment.
ing image-text pair purity. The Solver agent optimizes rea-                Through continuous interaction, the Solver improves geometric
soning through preference learning, with failure paths guid-               reasoning ability while the Generator enhances image generation
ing Teacher’s targeted augmentation. Independently, the                    capability, forming an optimization loop that advances both geo-
                                                                           metric reasoning and image synthesis.
Generator learns image generation capabilities on accumu-
lated ”image-code-instruction” triplets, distilling program-
matic drawing intelligence into visual generation. Start-
ing from only 108 seed problems, Socratic-Solver achieves                  of vision and language. As foundational capabilities ma-
49.11 on six geometric benchmarks using one-quarter of                     ture, multimodal mathematical reasoning has garnered sig-
baseline data, surpassing strong baselines by 2.43 points.                 nificant research attention [5, 21, 37], especially in geom-
Socratic-Generator achieves 42.4% on GenExam, estab-                       etry—a domain that demands both visual perception and
lishing new state-of-the-art for open-source models, sur-                  logical deduction. However, progress is severely bottle-
passing Seedream-4.0 (39.8%) and approaching Gemini-                       necked by the extreme scarcity of high-quality geometric
2.5-Flash-Image (43.1%).                                                   training data. Manual annotation is prohibitively expensive
                                                                           and time-consuming, while automated synthesis struggles
                                                                           to simultaneously balance correctness, diversity, and train-

    Figure 3. Overview of the Socratic-Geo interaction framework. The system operates as a closed loop centered on geometric data. (a) The
    Core Reasoning Loop: The Solver attempts to solve geometry problems. Its failures trigger the Teacher, which analyzes the reasoning
    gaps and programmatically invents a new, targeted problem. The new validated problem triplet is added back to the curriculum, enabling
    continuous self-improvement for the Solver. (b) The Synergistic Generation Byproduct: Independently, the Generator learns from high-
+   quality data produced during the Teacher’s invention process. For each new problem, the Teacher performs to create a descriptive drawing
    instruction. The Generator is trained on these instruction-image pairs, effectively distilling the Teacher’s programmatic intelligence.

Figure 4. A concrete instantiation of the Socratic-Geo interaction pipeline, where the Teacher transforms flawed reasoning into diagnostic
problems. Red highlighted regions mark critical intervention points including error diagnosis and geometric augmentation.
Left: The Solver incorrectly assumes a right triangle structure, overlooking the given constraint ∠BAC = 60◦ , leading to an invalid
solution path. Right: The Teacher introduces point P , forcing the Solver to apply the inscribed angle theorem combined with the 60◦
angle property to establish the relationship between ∠AP D and ∠ACD, directly targeting the reasoning deficiency.

Table 1. Evaluation of geometric data synthesis methods on six multimodal reasoning benchmarks: MathVerse, GeomVerse, GeoQA,
MathVision, MathVista, and WeMath. Performance is reported in Mean@1 (%). Data Scale” denotes the size of synthetic training data
in thousands (k), progressively growing across three curriculum stages. All results use LLM-as-judge (3-vote) evaluation. Arrow values
represent absolute point changes relative to Zero-shot baseline, where green arrows indicate performance improvements and red arrows
indicate performance declines. The Overall” column represents the average performance across five benchmarks (excluding GeomVerse).
Best results per category are highlighted in bold. Detailed configurations of the curriculum stages can be found in Appendix A.
